title: Salon grand
notes:
A pedalled salon grand — the piano a nocturne is played on. Its parent
`piano/felt-hammer` is the same room with the lid down and a cloth over the strings;
this one takes the cloth out, opens the lid, and holds the damper pedal.

**The felt comes off, and that is one number.** The parent's brief says it outright:
"drop it to a piano's usual 2-3 ms and the felt is gone no matter what the filter does".
So attack is 3 ms, four times faster, which is the largest single ratio in the fork and
therefore the separation that survives the lo-fi chain by itself. Everything below is
consequence.

**The pedal is the design.** Release 4.2 s against the parent's 1.8. A nocturne's left
hand is a wide arpeggio spanning a tenth, played once per bar at 60-76 bpm, and it is
*meant* to still be sounding when the next one starts - that overlap is the harmony, not
a smear. Decay 2.6 s to a 0.035 sustain: a longer string with less holding it up, because
a grand's note is nearly all tail. The parent decays in 1.4 s to 0.06, which is right for
a quiet upright and stops ringing before a slow bar is over.

**Polyphony 14, not 8.** With a 4.2 s release, six arpeggio notes a bar at 63 bpm leaves
roughly twenty notes alive at once. Eight steals voices mid-phrase and the bass of the
arpeggio - the note the ear is holding the chord by - is the oldest and so the first to
go. 14 is the cheapest number that survives a pedalled bar; it is not a section voice, so
the cost is linear in notes rather than multiplied.

**The hammer hill goes back.** The parent's most characteristic resonance is a -5 dB notch
at 3.2 kHz, the *absence* of hammer contact noise. Here it is +4 dB at 3.1 kHz - the
struck-string edge that lets a melody note carry over its own pedalled accompaniment.
Doing this by boost is against the usual advice in docs/voices.md, so it is not carrying
the separation: the envelope ratios are. It is a 9 dB swing on the parent's signature
band, which is enough to make the two unmistakable next to each other.

The rest of the box is a bigger one: 90 Hz case air (an upright's is 120 - a grand's is
longer and lower), 240 Hz soundboard, and a -4 dB notch at 780 Hz where the parent had a
+2 plate mode. That notch is the "open lid" - a real grand has less mid honk than an
upright, and per the docs a hole is more reliable contrast than a peak.

**`breath` moves from the mechanism to the hammer.** The parent's is 900 Hz at level 0.06
with a 4 ms follower: key bed, damper lift, a quiet room. This is 1900 Hz at 0.03 with a
1.5 ms follower - felt-on-wire contact, half as loud and twice as high, because on an open
grand the string wins and the click is only the leading edge. Breath centre is an axis the
lo-fi chain does not erode, so this is a second real separation after the envelopes.

**`vibrato` is still not vibrato.** Rate 1.2 Hz, depth 0.0045 - the parent's slow unison
beat, slightly faster and wider. A grand's three strings per note are further apart and
under more tension than an upright's, so they beat quicker. Still far below the threshold
of hearing it as modulation; it exists only so the pitch is not perfectly stationary.

**What this voice is not for.** Anything close, small or asleep - that is the parent, and
this one will sound stagey doing it. It also should not be asked to play block chords
below C3 with the pedal down: 90 Hz case air plus a 4.2 s release plus a fifth in the bass
is mud, and the fix is the voicing (wide, low root, nothing else under C3) rather than the
preset.
summary: Pedalled salon grand: 3 ms strike, 4.2 s release, hammer hill back at 3.1 kHz. The nocturne piano, for arpeggios that ring into each other.
